blocks.title: Formula Node Syntax Reference
paragraphs: A practical map of the syntax documented by NI. Create input/output terminals on the Formula Node border first, then reference those terminal names in the code.
[Open the official NI Formula Node syntax reference](https://www.ni.com/docs/en-US/bundle/labview/page/formula-node-syntax.html)
End each executable statement with `;`. Use braces to group a block. Both one-line and block comments are supported.

blocks.title: Statements, blocks, and comments

paragraphs: An assignment writes a value to an output, local variable, or array element. Expressions can use parentheses, function calls, array subscriptions, and the conditional `? :` form.

blocks.title: Assignments and expressions

paragraphs: Unary operators: `+ - ! ++ -- ~`. Use `==` to compare; a single `=` assigns.
Use `if`, `else`, `switch`, `case`, and `default` to choose behaviour.

blocks.title: Conditionals and selection

paragraphs: Formula Nodes support `for`, `while`, and `do ... while` loops. `break;` leaves the nearest loop or switch; `continue;` skips to the next loop iteration.

blocks.title: Loops and flow control

paragraphs: Declare a local variable with a type and identifier; arrays include a constant size in brackets.
Floating-point types: `float`, `float32`, `float64`. Integer types: `int`, `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `uInt8`, `uInt16`, `uInt32`.

blocks.title: Variables, arrays, and types

paragraphs: Identifiers begin with a letter or underscore, then may contain letters, digits, or underscores. Constants can be `pi`, decimal, binary (`0b...`), octal (leading `0`), hexadecimal (`0x...`), or floating-point values with an optional exponent such as `1.5e2`.

Use a function as `functionName(argument1, argument2)`. NI documents the available functions separately; only use functions supported by the installed LabVIEW version. Variables follow Formula Node scope rules, so declare locals in the block where they are needed and avoid reusing a terminal name for a local variable.
This reference is for Formula Node syntax only. Keep LabVIEW dataflow, wires, terminals, and local-variable configuration on the block diagram.

blocks.title: Concept anchor
paragraphs: LabVIEW does not send degrees directly to the servo. It calculates a pulse-width command; the servo electronics interpret that signal as a target position.

checkpoints.title: Lab scenario and setup
intro: You are building a local IoT motion-control node. The system must accept either a physical input from a potentiometer or an HMI command from LabVIEW, convert that command into a safe servo pulse width, and move a servo motor predictably. In automatic mode, the system performs a repeated waving motion based on speed and number of waves.

paragraphs: This lab focuses on the local motion-control and HMI layer of an IoT system. It does not yet upload motion data or commands to the cloud.

blocks.title: Central question
paragraphs: How does a voltage from a potentiometer or an HMI command become controlled servo motion?

items.title: Software
items.body: LabVIEW, NI LabVIEW LINX Toolkit, and LINX firmware loaded to Arduino.

items.title: Hardware
items.body: Arduino Mega, USB cable, breadboard, servo motor, potentiometer, 8 jumper wires, and the servo motor plastic arm attachment.

items.title: Required pins
items.body: Analog Pin 0 for potentiometer input. Digital Pin 7 for the servo signal.

blocks.title: Learning outcomes
items: **Servo wiring:** Identify servo power, ground, and signal wires.
**Safe circuit build:** Wire a servo motor and potentiometer to Arduino Mega safely.
**Analog input:** Read potentiometer voltage from A0 using LINX.
**Scaling:** Scale voltage to angle, then angle to servo pulse width.
**LINX servo control:** Use Servo Open, Servo Write, Servo Close, and LINX Close.
**HMI modes:** Build Manual and Automatic LabVIEW front panels.
**Automatic logic:** Use Case Structures, Formula Nodes, SubVIs, local variables, and previous-state values.
**Troubleshooting:** Diagnose wiring, scaling, servo-range, and LabVIEW logic faults.

blocks.title: If a wiring check fails
paragraphs: Disconnect power before correcting it, then recheck servo polarity, D7, A0, common ground, the arm attachment, and clearance around the moving shaft before powering again.

checkpoints.title: Open Arduino, read voltage, and command the servo
intro: Build the main VI that communicates with Arduino and the servo. Begin with a basic fixed pulse-width test before scaling.

blocks.alt: LabVIEW block diagram opening LINX and the servo channel, reading analog voltage inside a While Loop, writing a fixed pulse width, and closing both resources.
blocks.caption: Wire LINX Open, Servo Open, Analog Read, Set Pulse Width, Servo Close, and LINX Close in sequence.

paragraphs: Add LINX Open, create the Serial Port constant, and set it to COM3 or the correct Arduino COM port.
Add LINX Servo Open and set Servo Channel to `7`.
Place the loop, wire LINX resource and error tunnels, and create a Stop control.
Add LINX Analog Read inside the loop and set Analog Channel to `0`. Create a Voltage indicator.
Add Servo Write / Set Pulse Width inside the loop, set Servo Channel to `7`, and initially use `1000` microseconds.
Add Servo Close after the loop, then LINX Close. Wire resource and error lines through all blocks.

blocks.title: Find the safe pulse-width limits
paragraphs: Use the Manual control to increase or decrease the pulse width cautiously. Identify the lowest value that places the servo at approximately 0 degrees and the highest value that places it at approximately 180 degrees. Stop before the servo strains against its mechanical end stop, and record the two limits in the table in the next stage.

blocks.summary: If the fixed pulse-width test does not move safely
paragraphs: Stop the VI normally and disconnect power if the servo is blocked, hot, or driving against an end stop. Verify the LINX firmware and COM port, Servo Channel 7, Analog Channel 0, common ground, and wiring before changing one item and retesting.

checkpoints.title: Build the Manual/Automatic front panel and scale voltage to angle
intro: Add the front-panel HMI controls, then create the Manual case that turns potentiometer voltage into an angle command. For this first introduction to the structures, review the [Case Structure skill](kb:case-structure) and [Formula Node skill](kb:formula-node) in the course skill tree.

fields.label: What does the Case Structure decide?

blocks.alt: LabVIEW front panel with Choice Enum, Angle gauge, Speed and NumberOfWaves controls, GO button, Stop button, and Voltage indicator.
blocks.caption: Use this front panel as the visual reference for the Manual/Automatic HMI controls.

items.title: Enum
items.body: Name it `Choice`. Right-click the Enum control, choose **Properties**, open **Edit Items**, select **Insert**, and add `Manual` and `Automatic` as the two items.

items.title: Gauge
items.body: Find it in **Controls > Modern > Numeric > Gauge**. Name it `Angle`, then right-click the gauge, choose **Properties**, open the **Scale** tab, and set the scale range to 0–180 degrees.

items.title: Controls
items.body: Add `Speed` and `NumberOfWaves` as **Numeric controls**. Add `GO` as an **OK button**, and keep the `Voltage` indicator.

blocks.alt: LabVIEW Manual Case Structure selected by the Choice Enum, converting Voltage to Angle and sending the result to the Angle indicator
blocks.caption: This Case Structure view shows the Choice selector, the active Manual case, the voltage input, and the Angle output tunnel.

blocks.title: How the Manual case fits into the Case Structure
paragraphs: The Case Structure chooses which command path is active. Wire the `Choice` Enum to the selector terminal on the left side of the Case Structure; when the user selects `Manual`, LabVIEW displays and executes the Manual case, while `Automatic` will select the separate automatic-wave case later.

items.title: Inputs
items.body: The Manual case receives the potentiometer voltage from `Analog Read`. The `Choice` Enum is the selector input that determines which case is shown and executed.

items.title: Processing
items.body: Inside the Manual case, the Formula Node maps the 0-5 V input to a 0-180 degree command using `Angle = V / 5 * 180;`.

items.title: Output
items.body: Wire the Formula Node's `Angle` output to the Angle indicator and through the Case Structure output tunnel. This single angle output will then continue, on the next stage of this lab, to the shared pulse-width scaling and servo command.

blocks.title: Build sequence
paragraphs: Create the `Manual` and `Automatic` Enum items, wire `Choice` to the Case Structure selector, place the Formula Node in the Manual case, connect the voltage input and Angle output, then confirm that the Manual case produces one clean angle value for the next stage.

checkpoints.title: Convert angle into servo pulse width
intro: Place a Formula Node below the Case Structure so the Manual and Automatic cases share one angle-to-pulse-width conversion. The Case Structure should produce one numeric `Angle` value; the Formula Node should receive that value, apply the calibrated lower and upper pulse limits, and produce one numeric `PW` output for Set Pulse Width.

The mapping should preserve the endpoints: 0 degrees corresponds to your measured lower limit, 180 degrees corresponds to your measured upper limit, and intermediate angles scale proportionally between them. Use input and output terminals on the Formula Node border with names that match the block-diagram wiring.

blocks.alt: LabVIEW Case Structure and Formula Node showing Choice selecting Manual, Voltage converted to Angle, and Angle passed toward pulse-width scaling.
blocks.caption: Use this as a wiring and architecture reference: the Choice Enum selects the Manual case, the voltage is converted to an Angle, and that angle is passed to the shared pulse-width conversion. Recreate the structure with your own calibrated limits from Manual Control.

paragraphs: Add input `Angle`. Add output `PW`. Connect `PW` to the Pulse Width input of Set Pulse Width One Channel.

blocks.title: Use your recorded potentiometer range
paragraphs: Revisit the fully-left, middle, and fully-right voltages from Build Circuit. They are a physical reference for how the knob changes the Manual angle command. The direction may be reversed depending on which outside potentiometer terminal is connected to 5 V, but the Formula Node at this stage receives the resulting `Angle`, not the raw voltage. Use the three recorded positions to reason about the expected low, middle, and high pulse-width commands before testing.

blocks.title: Temporary Manual-case test
paragraphs: LabVIEW may show an error because the Automatic case does not yet have its input mapped. To test the Manual case only, temporarily wire the `Voltage` input directly to the `Angle` output in the Automatic case so the Case Structure is complete. This is only a temporary test connection; it is **not** the final Automatic-case implementation.

checkpoints.title: Create a reusable automatic-wave SubVI
intro: Create a new Blank VI for automatic waving. Add front-panel controls and indicators, then create a Formula Node using the [current NI documentation](https://www.ni.com/docs/en-US/bundle/labview/page/formula-node-syntax.html). Build and explain your own logic rather than copying a finished program.

blocks.alt: Wave Servo icon for the automatic waving SubVI.

blocks.title: Connector pane
paragraphs: Set a pattern with three inputs and one output. Top input to GO, middle to NumberOfWaves, bottom to Speed, output to Angle.
Copy this structure into the Formula Node after creating the listed terminals. The TODO comments deliberately leave the automatic-wave behaviour for you to implement and test.

blocks.title: Formula Node starter architecture

items.title: State inputs
items.body: Local variables changed to Read provide AngleLast, DirectionLast, WaveCountLast, and WavingLast.

blocks.title: Logic requirements
paragraphs: Initialize state from the previous values; use `GO` to begin a wave sequence; advance or reverse the angle according to direction; reverse at the safe limits; decrement the wave count at each completed pass; and stop when the requested count reaches zero. Document your own implementation.

blocks.title: Timing and icon
paragraphs: Add Wait with constant 10. Edit the icon, for example `Wave Servo`. Save the SubVI.
